messages.body_plain:
Hi Juan,

Please see code below.

Cheers,
Luis

library(dartRverse)
# function to introduce missing data randomly
# x is the genlight object
# p_imput is the percentage of missing data
introduce_Nas <- function(x,
                          p_imput) {
  x2 <- x
  matrix_NA <- as.matrix(x)
  geno <- expand.grid(1:nInd(x), 1:nLoc(x))
  geno_2 <-
    geno[sample(1:nrow(geno), nrow(geno) * (p_imput / 100)), ]
  matrix_NA[cbind(geno_2$Var1, geno_2$Var2)] <- NA
  # the variable below should be x2 at gen (without spaces)
  x2@gen <- lapply(1:nrow(matrix_NA), function(i)
    new("SNPbin", as.integer(matrix_NA[i,])))
  return(x2)
}
# filtering on missing data
t1 <- gl.filter.callrate(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>, threshold = 1)
gl.smearplot(t1)
t2 <- introduce_Nas(t1, p_imput = 50)
gl.smearplot(t2)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrian,

The method used to calculate the Genomic Relationship Matrix (GRM) involves centering the allele content for each locus using allele frequencies across all individuals in your dataset. This means that if your dataset has genetic structure (i.e., contains different populations), the off-diagonal values in the GRM can be less than zero or greater than one. For example, see Figure 1 in Endelman, J. B. , Jannink, J.-L. (2012). Shrinkage estimation of the realized relationship matrix. G3: Genes, Genomics, Genetics 2, 1405.

Values greater than one indicate a higher-than-expected genetic similarity between individuals—in other words, these individuals share more alleles identical by state than the average in the population. Conversely, values less than zero suggest that individuals are less related than the average pair in the population.

I recommend starting with a threshold of 0.5 when interpreting the GRM. After applying this threshold, compare the results with those from the gl.report.replicates function. This comparison will help you adjust the threshold accordingly.

Cheers,
Luis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jean,

A good place to start is by reading our tutorials, see particularly tutorial 5:

http://georges.biomatix.org/dartR

Here are some examples:

library(dartRverse)
t1 <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
# assign chromosome
t1$chromosome <- t1$other$loc.metrics$Chrom_Platypus_Chrom_NCBIv1
# assign Snp position
t1$position <- t1$other$loc.metrics$ChromPos_Platypus_Chrom_NCBIv1
# Table of chromosomes
# the name of unknown chromosomes (SNPs that were not mapped to a reference genome)
# appear empty in the below table ie ""
table(t1$chromosome)
# get index of loci with unknown chromosomes
unknown_chr <- which(t1$chromosome == "")
# remove loci with unknown chromosomes
t2 <- gl.drop.loc(t1,loc.list = locNames(t1)[unknown_chr])
# check the first 10 SNP positions
# loci with unknown position have a 0 position
head(t1$position,10)
# get index of loci with unknown position
unknown_pos <- which(t1$position == 0)
# remove loci with unknown position
t3 <- gl.drop.loc(t1,loc.list = locNames(t1)[unknown_pos])
# remove loci for which the missing data  is more than 80%
t4 <- gl.filter.callrate(t1,threshold = 0.8)

Cheers,
Luis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rizki,

To test if a pair of individuals are true parent-offspring, you can use our updated functions gl.report.parent.offspring and gl.filter.parent.offspring which you can install using:

devtools::install_github("green-striped-gecko/dartR.captive@dev")

These functions examine the frequency of pedigree inconsistent loci, that is, those loci that are homozygotes in the parent for the reference allele, and homozygous in the offspring for the alternate allele (and viceversa).

To check which loci are inconsistent with a parent-offspring relationship in a pair of individuals, you can use the code below:

library(dartRverse)
x <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
r1 <- gl.report.parent.offspring(x,
                                 min.rdepth = 12,
                                 min.reproducibility = 1,
                                 range = 2)
r1
# The first pair of individuals that had only one incompatible locus
ind_to_test <- unlist(unname(r1[3,c("ind1","ind2")]))
# subsetting individuals
ind_to_test2 <- which(indNames(x)%in%ind_to_test)
test_mat <- t(as.data.frame(as.matrix(x)[ind_to_test2,]))
# testing which loci are incompatible with a parent-offspring relationship
# ie homozygotes for the reference allele in one individual and
# homozygotesfor the alternate allele in the other individuals (and viceversa).
test1 <- unname(which(test_mat[,1] == 0 & test_mat[,2] == 2))
test2 <- unname(which(test_mat[,1] == 2 & test_mat[,2] == 0))
# subsetting incompatible loci
mismatch <- test_mat[c(test1,test2),]
# Note that there are more incompatible loci here because the function
# gl.report.parent.offspring filters on read depth and reproducibility
mismatch

Cheers,
Luis

# identifying duplicated individuals

dup <- gl.report.replicates(t1,

# here is the SNP position information

Hi,

Please see code below to merge two datasets with different individuals and the same loci.

Cheers,
Luis

library(dartRverse)
t1 <- gl.load("data1.rds")
nLoc(t1)
# [1] 400
nInd(t1)
# [1] 20
t2 <- gl.load("data2.rds")
nLoc(t2)
# [1] 400
nInd(t2)
# [1] 20
# the datasetshave the same loci but different individuals
# the sum below should be equal to 0
sum(locNames(t1) == locNames(t2))
# [1] 0
class(t1) <- "genlight"
class(t2) <- "genlight"
merge_gl <- rbind.genlight(t1,t2)
merge_gl$other$loc.metrics <- rbind(t1$other$loc.metrics)
merge_gl$other$ind.metrics <- rbind(t1$other$ind.metrics,
                                    t2$other$ind.metrics)

merge_gl <- gl.compliance.check(merge_gl)
# adding information of the SNP position within the Trimmed Sequence
merge_gl$position <- as.integer(merge_gl$other$loc.metrics$SnpPosition)

gl2fasta(merge_gl,
         method=3,
         outfile ="output.fasta",

         outpath=getwd())

> > Hi Anna,

> > Sorry for the late reply.

> > You can calculate the effective number of alleles using the dartR function gl.report.diversity(), as shown in the code below. This function is based on the paper of Bill Sherwin:
> > Sherwin, William B., et al. "Information theory broadens the spectrum of molecular ecology and evolution." Trends in ecology & evolution 32.12 (2017): 948-963.
> >
> > The effective number of alleles is very sensitive to rare alleles and unequal sample sizes, so it can be biased if you don't have a large sample size. The best way to deal with this is calculating allelic richness using the rarefaction method as implemented in the package Hierfstat, as shown in the code below. If you want to know more about how allelic richness is calculated, see:
> > El Mousadik, A., and R. J. Petit. "High level of genetic differentiation for allelic richness among populations of the argan tree [Argania spinosa (L.) Skeels] endemic to Morocco." Theoretical and applied genetics 92.7 (1996): 832-839.
> >
> >
> > library(dartR)
> > test <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
> > res <- gl.report.diversity(test)
> > # this is the effective number of alleles
> > res_2 <- res$zero_D_alpha
> > # printing results
> > res_2
> >
> > library(hierfstat)
> > test_2 <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
> > # filtering loci with all missing data
> > test_2 <- gl.filter.allna(test_2)
> > #converting to genind
> > genind_2 <- gl2gi(test_2)
> > #converting to hierfstat
> > hierfstat <- genind2hierfstat(genind_2)
> > # calculating allelic richness
> > res_3 <- allelic.richness(hierfstat)
> > # calculating mean by column
> > res_4 <- colMeans(res_3$Ar,na.rm = TRUE)
> > #printing results
> > res_4
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Luis
> >
> >
> >

alpha_val <- 0.05

  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = ifelse(is.na <http://is.na>(unique(res$data$pop, fromLast = T)), 21, 19))))+

> > > > > The method used to calculate the Genomic Relationship Matrix (GRM) involves centering the allele content for each locus using allele frequencies across all individuals in your dataset. This means that if your dataset has genetic structure (i.e., contains different populations), the off-diagonal values in the GRM can be less than zero or greater than one. For example, see Figure 1 in Endelman, J. B. , Jannink, J.-L. (2012). Shrinkage estimation of the realized relationship matrix. G3: Genes, Genomics, Genetics 2, 1405.
> > > > >
> > > > > Values greater than one indicate a higher-than-expected genetic similarity between individuals—in other words, these individuals share more alleles identical by state than the average in the population. Conversely, values less than zero suggest that individuals are less related than the average pair in the population.
> > > > >
> > > > > I recommend starting with a threshold of 0.5 when interpreting the GRM. After applying this threshold, compare the results with those from the gl.report.replicates function. This comparison will help you adjust the threshold accordingly.
